Testimony in SUPPORT of LD 1734, An Act to Exempt Over-the-counter Medicines from the Sales and Use Tax
Committee on Taxation May 14, 2025
Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and Esteemed Members of the Taxation Committee,
My name is Madeleine DesFosses, and I am submitting this testimony on behalf of the Maine Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics. We are in support of LD 1734, which will help to make over-the-counter (OTC) medications more affordable for Maine families.
In Maine, prescription medications are currently tax-exempt, as they are considered essential. However, over-the-counter medications are also essential, but are subjected to the 5.5% general sales tax, which may be burdensome and prohibitive for many families in Maine. OTC medications may be needed to treat or relieve the symptoms of a cold that lasts only a few days, or may be needed for a long-term or chronic condition that an individual needs to use for months, years, or their lifetime. No matter the situation, individuals and families deserve to access medications at the lowest cost possible.
For a family struggling financially, the cost of OTC medications can be insurmountable. For example, for the OTC allergy medication Claritin costs 35 dollars before tax for a 45-count bottle, an amount that is simply unaffordable for many Mainers no matter how much they may need the medication. To make matters worse, the federal government is considering tariffs on imported medications, which could increase prices and worsen the financial burden placed on families.
Accessible and affordable OTC medications not only save Maine families money, but also saves our healthcare system dollars. In fact, it is estimated that every 1 dollar spent on OTC medications saves the US healthcare system 7 dollars, or 146 million dollars annually (1). The majority of these cost savings come from reduced clinical visits as a result of OTC medications being readily available to the public. Making OTC medications tax-exempt would make these medications more accessible, thereby saving families and the healthcare system valuable dollars.
While a 5.5% tax may not seem like a prohibitive cost to some, for many Mainers struggling financially, that extra cost can mean the difference between affording an OTC medication and going without. We must ensure that every Mainer can afford the medications they need. OTC medications aren't a luxury, they're a necessity.
We urge the committee to vote "Ought to Pass" on LD 1734.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Madeleine DesFosses Advocacy and Public Health Manager, Maine AAP

References:
1. Consumer Healthcare Products Association. Value of OTC Medicines to the U.S. Healthcare System. March 2019. Accessed May 14, 2025. https://www.chpa.org/sites/default/files/media/docs/2020-10/Value-of-OTCMedicines-to-the-US-Healthcare-System-03012019.pdf

Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee
on Taxation, my name is Mattie Daughtry. I serve as President of the Maine Senate and proudly
represent Senate District 23, including Brunswick, Freeport, Harpswell, Pownal, Chebeague Island,
and part of Yarmouth. I am pleased to be here today to introduce LD 1734, "An Act to Exempt
Over-the-counter Medicines from the Sales and Use Tax."
The goal of this legislation is simple but meaningful: to lower everyday costs for Maine families
who continue to feel the squeeze of high prices. While we are fortunate that many aspects of our economy have recovered from the early 2020s pandemic, the reality is that for too many Mainers,
essential items like medicine still strain household budgets.
Currently, prescription medicines are exempt from Maine's sales and use tax, but over-the-counter
(OTC) medicines---despite being just as essential for maintaining health---are not. LD 1734 updates
our tax code to exempt a range of over-the-counter medicines, such as cough and cold treatments, allergy medications, eye and ear preparations, contraceptives, opioid antagonists, and other critical health products. These are items families rely on every day to stay healthy, prevent illness, and manage chronic conditions.
This bill makes a commonsense change that will make it a little easier for Mainers to care for '
themselves and their loved ones without the added burden of a sales tax at the register. In a time
when families are working hard to stretch every dollar, this small but targeted exemption would put
meaningful savings back into their pockets.
I also want to highlight that LD 1734 is carefully crafted. It ties eligibility for the exemption to the
U.S. Food and Drug Administration's labeling standards, ensuring clarity for retailers and consumers alike while keeping the exemption focused on legitimate, medically necessary products.
I respectfully ask for the Committee's support to move this bill forward. Thank you for your time
and consideration, and I am happy to answer any questions.

TESTIMONY OF MICHAEL J. ALLEN, ASSOCIATE COMMISSIONER FOR TAX POLICY
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE AND FINANCIAL SERVICES
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation Hearing Date: May 14, 2025, Wednesday at 1:30 P.M.
LD 1734 - "An Act to Exempt Over-the-counter Medicines from the Sales and Use Tax"
Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and members of the Taxation Committee - good afternoon, my name is Michael Allen, Associate Commissioner for Tax Policy in the Department of Administrative and Financial Services. I am testifying at the request of the Administration Against LD 1734, "An Act to Exempt Over-the-counter Medicines from the Sales and Use Tax."
The bill would expand the current sales and use tax exemption for medicines sold on a doctor's prescription to include medicine sold "over-the-counter" where the medicine is "subject to the format and content requirements of the U.S. FDA under 21 C.F.R. � 201.66." The bill defines the term "over-the-counter medicine or drug" to mean anesthetics, antacids, anthelmintics, antibacterial, antifungal and antiviral medicine, antiseptics, astringents, contraceptive supplies (including drugs), devices and products approved by the FDA to prevent pregnancy, emetics and antiemetics, medication prepared for use in the eyes, ears or nose, opioid antagonists, products intended to be taken for coughs, colds, asthma or allergies, and steroidal medicines.
The revenue loss associated with this proposal would be substantial. A more cost-effective approach would be to increase the Sales Tax Fairness Credit to provide sales tax relief to taxpayers truly overburdened by sales tax.
1

Should the Committee move forward with the bill as drafted, it should be amended to include an effective date in the exemption text by adding "on or after January 1, 2026," within proposed paragraph B. Additionally, the Committee should consider whether it intends the reference to 21 C.F.R. � 201.66 to cause static or rolling conformity to federal law - either incorporating the C.F.R. provision as of a certain date, or automatically incorporating all future amendments to that section of the C.F.R.
I will further note that tying the exemption to 21 C.F.R. � 201.66 ("Format and content requirements for over-the-counter (OTC) drug product labeling") would exclude items such as vitamins and other supplements, which are instead subject to the FDA food labeling requirements under 21 C.F.R., Part 101 ("Food Labeling"). This may be intended.
The Administration looks forward to working with the Committee on the bill; representatives from MRS will be here for the Work Session to provide additional information and respond in detail to the Committee's questions.

Testimony of Representative Kilton Webb in support of
LD 1734, An Act to Exempt Over-the-counter Medicines from the Sales and Use Tax
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation
Good afternoon, Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier and members of the Taxation Committee. My name is Kilton Webb, and I represent House District 98, which includes Durham, Pownal and parts of Bowdoin, Lisbon and Topsham. I am honored to be the lead cosponsor of LD 1734, An Act to Exempt Over-the-counter Medicines from the Sales and Use Tax.
This bill adds over-the-counter (OTC), FDA-approved medicines and drugs to Maine's list of sales tax exemptions. This would include anesthetics, antacids, contraceptive supplies, opioid antagonists as well as medicines intended to be taken for coughs, colds, asthma or allergies.
Right now in Maine, an OTC medication that is not sold on a doctor's prescription is taxable, even if it is purchased on the recommendation of a physician. However, there is no tax on nonprescription medicines purchased by a doctor for use in the doctor's medical practice.
We are seeing other states begin to follow suit. OTC medicine is generally tax-exempt in nine states including Florida, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Texas, Vermont, Virginia as well as Washington, D.C. We have the opportunity to join these states in helping to cut the cost our community members are paying for their OTC medications.
Mainers are looking for ways to reduce the burden of inflation and rising prices on items they buy regularly, and we need to help them. LD 1734 would do just this.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

District 98: Durham, Pownal, and parts of Bowdoin, Lisbon and Topsham

Dear Chairs Grohoski and Cloutier:
On behalf of the Consumer Healthcare Products Association (CHPA)1, I'm writing to express strong support for LD 1734. This critical legislation expands access to nonprescription medicines for Maine residents by exempting these essential healthcare products from sales and use tax.
Over-the-counter (OTC) medications are essential for managing everyday health needs. From headaches and allergies to cold symptoms and minor injuries, these products help Mainers function effectively at work, school, and home. By removing the sales tax burden, we make these necessities more affordable for all. Research indicates that the average U.S. household spends $645 annually on OTC products.2 Exempting OTC medicines from sales tax would provide significant savings to Maine consumers, enhancing access to early treatment options. These savings are especially impactful for low-income residents who rely heavily on OTCs for their healthcare needs.
OTC medicines also reduce strain on our healthcare system. When people can safely treat minor conditions at home, they reduce unnecessary doctor and emergency room visits. This is especially important in rural areas of Maine where healthcare access can be limited. Studies show that every $1 spent on OTC medicines saves the U.S. healthcare system over $7, amounting to $146 billion in savings annually.3 By making self-care more affordable and accessible, OTC medications help reduce the burden on the healthcare system, allowing it to allocate resources to more serious conditions that require physician intervention.
